- **The default settings document** (`settings.DefaultSettingsJSON(registry)`, `emetos-virtual:/defaultSettings.json`, language `jsonc`, tab "Default Settings"): one JSONC object with every registered setting once, grouped by the groups of the editor in their order (Commonly Used left out), indented with a tab, "\n" lines. A group is announced by a comment with its path ("// Text Editor > Font"); a setting is its description as `//` comments wrapped at 80 columns (Markdown as it is written), then, when they apply, "Allowed values: …" with a line "  value: description" for each described value, "Minimum: n", "Maximum: n" and "Deprecated: …", then `"key": default,` with the default as JSON (objects and arrays indented one level more) and a blank line before the next setting. There is no trailing comma. The default blocks of the languages (`"[go]": {…}`) are not in it.
- **Not built in step 8.2**: the filters `@tag:`, `@feature:`, `@ext:`, `@hasPolicy` and `@stable` (ignored with a hint), the suggestions dropdown of the filters and the filter menu of the search box, the fuzzy and remote (natural language) search and VS Code's match types and TF-IDF ordering, the 200 ms delay of the search, `@id:` without regard to case, "Open Folder Settings" and "Configure Language Specific Settings", the `edit` flag of `revealSetting` (adding the property to the file), the `[language]` blocks of the defaults in the default settings document, the "(Also modified in: …)" notes in the language view, and a target for language blocks other than the tab (the Workspace tab edits the workspace file's block).

### 11.2 Commands and context keys (`core/command`, `core/contextkey`)

- Commands have an id (VS Code's ids where the command exists in VS Code), a title, a category, a precondition, and a handler. The registry holds metadata first; the handler is attached by the package that implements it (an editor command's handler lives in `gui/editor` and calls `core/edit`). Menus, keybindings, the palette and dev commands all run commands by id, with optional JSON-compatible arguments. A command VS Code does not list in the palette (the cursor commands) has no title, and the palette skips it. Setting a handler on a command that has one stacks it: the last one runs, and its remover brings the previous one back. `Run` does not check the precondition; menus, the palette and the dispatcher call `Enabled` first, as VS Code does.
- **Menus** hold items that run commands by id (§10.1 "Menus and the menu bar"). A command that VS Code puts in a menu gets its row in `command/menus_default.go` with VS Code's menu id, group, order, `when` and mnemonic title; the menus show an item dimmed when the precondition of its command does not hold and leave it out when its `when` does not. The built-in menus have rows for the commands that exist, and a menu appears in the menu bar when it has a row.
- Context keys (e.g. `editorTextFocus`, `editorHasSelection`, `findWidgetVisible`, `explorerViewletFocus`, `resourceExtname`) live in scopes: a tree of scopes (window → part → widget); a widget gets a child scope from its parent's and sets its keys there; a lookup walks up the tree; the dispatcher (§5.4) evaluates against the scope of the focused widget. When-clauses use VS Code's syntax: `!`, `&&`, `||`, `==`, `!=`, `=~` (regex), `<`, `>`, `in`, `not in`, parentheses. Evaluation follows JavaScript's rules where VS Code relies on them (`==` is loose, a key that is not set is tested as the string "undefined" by `=~`, `<` and `>` parse the value as a float). Expressions are kept in VS Code's normal form (flat, sorted, `||` outermost) so that `Negate`, `Equals` and `Implies` behave as in VS Code. Regular expressions use Go's engine until `core/regex` has its ECMAScript mode; a pattern it cannot run (lookahead, backreferences) is accepted and never matches.
- The notification host sets `notificationCenterVisible`, `notificationToastsVisible` and `notificationFocus` on the window's keys (step 6.11, §10.7); the Escape rules of `notifications.hideList` and `notifications.hideToasts` have their `when` on them.
- The status bar (step 6.20, §10.1) registers `workbench.action.editor.changeLanguageMode` (Change Language Mode, Ctrl+K M), `workbench.action.editor.changeEOL` (Change End of Line Sequence), `workbench.action.editor.changeEncoding` (Change File Encoding) and `changeEditorIndentation` (no title); the window binds them while the shell is on screen. The setting `files.associations` (an object, default `{}`) is the one the language picker writes. It also registers the colors `statusBarItem.activeBackground`, `hoverBackground`, `hoverForeground`, `compactHoverBackground`, `focusBorder`, `prominentForeground`, `prominentBackground`, `prominentHoverForeground`, `prominentHoverBackground`, `errorBackground`, `errorForeground`, `errorHoverForeground`, `errorHoverBackground`, the same four for `warning`, and `errorForeground`. It sets no context key. The source of a command run by a click on an item is `command.SourceStatusBar`.
- The editor group sets `activeEditor` (the type id of the active input, unset with none), `activeEditorIsPinned` (the active tab is sticky) and `activeEditorIsNotPreview` on the window's keys (step 6.8, §10.3); the Close Editor row of the File menu has the precondition `activeEditor`. The grid of groups (step 6.9) adds `multipleEditorGroups`, `editorPartMultipleEditorGroups`, `editorPartMaximizedEditorGroup` and `activeEditorGroupEmpty`; the Switch Group rows and `toggleMaximizeEditorGroup` have their preconditions on them and Ctrl+W has a second rule, `closeGroup`, under `activeEditorGroupEmpty && multipleEditorGroups`.

- Saving (step 7.1, §6.3) registers `workbench.action.files.save` (Save, Ctrl+S), `workbench.action.files.saveAs` (Save As..., Ctrl+Shift+S), `workbench.action.files.saveWithoutFormatting` (Save without Formatting, Ctrl+K S on Linux; it skips every save participant, since there is no formatter), `saveAll` (VS Code's id of Save All; no key on Linux: VS Code gives Ctrl+K S to it on Windows only) and `workbench.action.files.saveAll` (Save All in the palette, which runs it), `workbench.action.files.revert` (Revert File) and `workbench.action.files.newUntitledFile` (New Untitled Text File, Ctrl+N; its argument may be `{"languageId": "go"}`). The File menu has New Text File (`1_new`), Save, Save As... and Save All (`4_save`; enabled by `activeEditor` and `dirtyWorkingCopies`) and Revert File (`6_close`, `activeEditorCanRevert`). Settings: `files.trimTrailingWhitespace`, `files.insertFinalNewline`, `files.trimFinalNewlines`, `files.defaultLanguage` and `files.saveConflictResolution` (`files.encoding` and `files.eol` were registered before). Context keys: `activeEditorIsDirty`, `activeEditorCanRevert`, `dirtyWorkingCopies`. The commands act on the tab their argument names (the menus of a tab) or on the active editor.
- Closing (step 7.2, §10.3, §10.10, §10.11) registers `workbench.action.closeWindow` (Close Workspace Tab since step 9b.1, "Close Window" before, in the palette; Alt+F4 and Ctrl+Shift+W on Linux; File menu row "Clos&&e Workspace Tab" since step 9b.2, group `6_close`, order 4) and `workbench.action.quit` (no title, so no palette entry, as VS Code; Ctrl+Q; File menu row "E&&xit" titled "Exit", group `z_Exit`, order 1), both bound by the shell to `Window.RequestClose`; and the setting `files.hotExit` (§10.10). The existing close commands ask about unsaved changes. No context key is added.
- Auto save (step 7.3, §6.3) registers `workbench.action.toggleAutoSave` (Toggle Auto Save, category File, in the palette, no key; File menu row "A&&uto Save", group `5_autosave`, order 1, toggled by `config.files.autoSave != 'off'`, the `Toggled` condition of a menu row, §10.1) and the settings `files.autoSave`, `files.autoSaveDelay`, `files.autoSaveWorkspaceFilesOnly` and `files.autoSaveWhenNoErrors`. No context key is added. The settings are context keys of the form `config.<setting>` in every `when` the window evaluates: the menus (`menuContext`) and, since this step, the key dispatcher (`Window.DispatchKey` evaluates a keybinding's `when` in the scope of the focused widget over the settings), as VS Code's configuration keys; a key of the scope wins over a setting of the same name.
- Restore and recent lists (step 7.5, §10.10) register `workbench.action.openRecent` (Open Recent..., category File, in the palette; Ctrl+R on Linux, VS Code's key; File menu row "&&More..." in the Open Recent submenu, group `y_more`), `workbench.action.clearRecentFiles` (Clear Recently Opened..., category File, in the palette, no key; row "&&Clear Recently Opened..." in the submenu, group `z_clear`), and `openRecentFolder` and `openRecentFile` (no title, so not in the palette; the rows of the recent folders and files run them with the path as the argument); the File menu has the submenu row "Open &&Recent" (group `2_open`, order 4, VS Code's) whose rows are the dynamic ones of `MenuRegistry.SetProvider` plus Reopen Closed Editor (group `1_editor`, order 1). The settings are `window.restoreWindows` (`preserve`, `all`, `folders`, `one`, `none`; default `all`; application scope) and `window.restoreFullscreen` (default false; application scope). No context key is added.
- Zoom, full screen, zen mode and the centered layout (step 8.5, §10.9) register `workbench.action.zoomIn` (Zoom In, Ctrl+=, Ctrl+Shift+=, Ctrl+NumPad_Add), `zoomOut` (Zoom Out, Ctrl+-, Ctrl+NumPad_Subtract), `zoomReset` (Reset Zoom, Ctrl+NumPad0), `toggleFullScreen` (Toggle Full Screen, F11), `toggleZenMode` (Toggle Zen Mode, Ctrl+K Z), `exitZenMode` (no title; Escape Escape when `inZenMode`) and `toggleCenteredLayout` (Toggle Centered Layout, no key), all with the category View but `exitZenMode`; the View > Appearance rows of §10.9; the settings `window.zoomLevel`, `window.zoomPerWindow`, `zenMode.fullScreen`, `zenMode.centerLayout`, `zenMode.showTabs`, `zenMode.hideStatusBar`, `zenMode.hideActivityBar`, `zenMode.hideLineNumbers`, `zenMode.restore`, `zenMode.silentNotifications`, `workbench.editor.centeredLayoutAutoResize` and `workbench.editor.centeredLayoutFixedWidth` (VS Code's defaults and texts; `zenMode.hideTabs` is not registered). The window sets the context keys `isFullscreen`, `inZenMode` and `isCenteredLayout`. The handlers are the window's (`gui/app/zoom.go`, `zen.go`).
- Windows (step 7.8, §10.11) register `workbench.action.newWindow` (New Workspace Tab since step 9b.1, in the palette, Ctrl+Shift+N, File menu row "New &&Workspace Tab" since step 9b.2, group `1_new`, order 3) and `workbench.action.switchWindow` (Switch Window..., in the palette, no key), and the settings `window.openFoldersInNewWindow` (`on`, `off`, `default`; default `default`), `window.openFilesInNewWindow` (`on`, `off`, `default`; default `off`) and `window.newWindowDimensions` (`default`, `inherit`, `offset`, `maximized`, `fullscreen`; default `default`), all of application scope, with VS Code's texts. The window has its own registry of commands (§5.1); the commands about windows are bound when the window is made. No context key is added.
- The tray (step 9b.4, §10.14) registers the setting `window.closeToTray` (application scope, boolean, default `true`; Emetos's own, VS Code has no tray). No command, key or menu is added: the tray's items run the manager's methods and `emetos.workspaceTab.openFolder`.
- Workspace tabs (step 9b.2, §10.14) register `emetos.workspaceTab.close` (Close Workspace Tab), `.closeOthers` (Close Other Workspace Tabs), `.closeToTheRight` (Close Workspace Tabs to the Right), `.copyPath` (Copy Path of Workspace Tab), `.revealInFileManager` (Reveal Workspace Tab in File Manager) and `.openFolder` (Open Folder in New Workspace Tab...), all in the palette under the category Workspace and without a key (step 9b.5 added the keys and the commands that switch and move tabs: `.next` (Next Workspace Tab, Ctrl+Alt+PageDown), `.previous` (Previous Workspace Tab, Ctrl+Alt+PageUp), `.open1` ... `.open9` (no title, so not in the palette; Ctrl+Alt+1 ... 9), `.switch` (Switch Workspace Tab...) and `.moveLeft`/`.moveRight` (Move Workspace Tab Left/Right, no key), all category Workspace, and the View submenu `MenubarWorkspaceTabsMenu`; see "As built (step 9b.5)"). Each of the first five acts on the tab its argument `{"tabId"}` names (the menu of a tab gives it), else on the tab of the workspace that runs it. The menus `WorkspaceTabContext` (Close, Close Others, Close to the Right; Copy Path, Reveal in File Manager; Switch Profile... (`workbench.profiles.actions.switchProfile`), in groups `1_close`, `2_path`, `3_profile`) and `WorkspaceTabNew` (Workspace..., the `.openFolder` command, group `1_new`) hold their rows. The menu of a tab is evaluated with the keys `workspaceTabCount`, `workspaceTabIsLast` and `activeWorkspaceTabHasFolder` set for the tab that was clicked (step 9b.5 also sets `workspaceTabCount`, `activeWorkspaceTabHasFolder`, `workspaceTabIsFirst` and `workspaceTabIsLast` as keys of every workspace, for the active tab). The colors `titleBar.inactiveBackground` and `titleBar.inactiveForeground` (VS Code's defaults) and the value `compact` of `window.menuBarVisibility` (now the default) are registered.
- External changes (step 7.4, §6.3) register no command and no key, and set no context key. They register the setting `workbench.editor.decorations.colors` (boolean, true, window scope, VS Code's description "Controls whether editor file decorations should use colors.") and the color `list.errorForeground` (§10.3); `workbench.editor.closeOnFileDelete` (step 6.15) is used as before. The notification buttons (Overwrite, Revert) are notification actions, not commands.
- The panels set `activePanel`, `problemsVisibility`, `focusedView`, `problemFocus`, `problemsFilterFocus`, `problems.filter.errors`, `problems.filter.warnings`, `problems.filter.info`, `problems.filter.activeFile`, `inOutput`, `outputView.scrollLock` and `activeOutputChannel` on the window's keys (step 6.12, §10.13); the Ctrl+F, Ctrl+Down and Escape rules of the Problems view have their `when` on `focusedView` and `problemsFilterFocus`.
- The quick input sets `inQuickOpen`, `inQuickInput`, `inputFocus` and `quickInputType` (`"quickPick"`) on the window's keys while it is open, and the key of the mode that is active (`inCommandsPicker` for `>`, `inViewsPicker` for `view `; a provider names it in `ProviderInfo.ContextKey`) (step 6.17, §10.6). Its Escape rules have their `when` on `inQuickOpen`. The `CommandPalette` menu has no row that shows: a row of it whose `when` does not hold keeps its command out of the palette (VS Code's `f1: false`), and the palette also leaves out the commands that need an editor while none is open.
- The file mode of the quick input sets `inFilesPicker` (step 6.18, §10.6) while it is the active mode, as VS Code's `defaultQuickAccessContextKeyValue`; no keybinding has it in its `when`.
- The editor modes of the quick input set `inEditorsPicker` while one is active (step 6.19, §10.6); the keys that move in the switcher (`quickOpenNavigateNextInEditorPicker`, `quickOpenNavigatePreviousInEditorPicker`) have `inQuickOpen && inEditorsPicker` as their `when`. The history sets `canNavigateBack`, `canNavigateForward`, `canNavigateBackInNavigationLocations`, `canNavigateForwardInNavigationLocations`, `canNavigateToLastNavigationLocation`, `canNavigateBackInEditLocations`, `canNavigateForwardInEditLocations`, `canNavigateToLastEditLocation` and `canReopenClosedEditor` (step 6.19, §10.3); Go Back and Go Forward have the first two in their `when` and their menu rows are dimmed by them, and the Ctrl+Tab keys have `!activeEditorGroupEmpty`.
- The settings editor (step 8.1, §10.3, §11.1) registers `workbench.action.openSettings` (title "Settings", Ctrl+, with no `when`; rows "&&Settings" in the Preferences submenu of the File menu, group `2_configuration`, order 2, and in the Manage menu; the palette leaves it out, as VS Code does), `workbench.action.openSettings2` ("Preferences: Open Settings (UI)", the palette's entry; it runs the same) and `workbench.action.openWorkspaceSettings` ("Preferences: Open Workspace Settings", in the palette while `workbenchState != 'empty'`; it opens the Workspace tab). The File menu has the submenu row "&&Preferences" (group `5_autosave`, order 2). The argument of the first two is the text of the search (a string or `{"query": "..."}`); an open settings editor is revealed (VS Code's target of `openSettings` is the user's, so the tab goes back to User) and its search box gets the focus. The setting `workbench.settings.editor` (`ui` or `json`, default `ui`; window scope) says which editor Ctrl+, opens. The colors are those of §11.1. No context key is added.
- The JSON commands of the settings (step 8.2, §7.1, §11.1) register `workbench.action.openSettingsJson` ("Open User Settings (JSON)"), `workbench.action.openWorkspaceSettingsFile` ("Open Workspace Settings (JSON)"; palette `when workbenchState != 'empty'`), `workbench.action.openRawDefaultSettings` ("Open Default Settings (JSON)") and `workbench.action.openGlobalSettings` ("Open User Settings"), all in the category Preferences and in the palette (as VS Code's `f1`); none has a key or a menu row (the File > Preferences menu has Settings only, as VS Code's). `openSettingsJson` and `openWorkspaceSettingsFile` take `{"revealSetting": {"key": "..."}}`; `openSettings`, `openSettings2` and `openGlobalSettings` also take the same object as the search `@id:<key>`. No setting or context key is added.
- The keybindings editor (step 8.3, §11.3) registers `workbench.action.openGlobalKeybindings` ("Open Keyboard Shortcuts", category Preferences, Ctrl+K Ctrl+S; row "&&Keyboard Shortcuts" in the Preferences submenu of the File menu and in the Manage menu, group `2_configuration`, order 4), `workbench.action.openGlobalKeybindingsFile` ("Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)") and `workbench.action.openDefaultKeybindingsFile` ("Open Default Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)"), all in the palette. The first takes the text of the search (a string or `{"query": "..."}`). The commands of the editor, `keybindings.editor.searchKeybindings` (Ctrl+F), `clearSearchResults` ("Clear Search Results", Escape; the only one with a title, and the palette leaves it out), `recordSearchKeys` (Alt+K), `focusKeybindings` (Ctrl+Down), `defineKeybinding` (Enter), `addKeybinding` (Ctrl+K Ctrl+A), `defineWhenExpression` (Ctrl+K Ctrl+E), `removeKeybinding` (Delete), `resetKeybinding`, `showConflicts`, `copyKeybindingEntry` (Ctrl+C), `copyCommandKeybindingEntry` and `copyCommandTitle` have no title (they are not in the palette), all with the weight of the workbench contributions. The editor sets the context keys `inKeybindings` (the focus is in the editor), `inKeybindingsSearch` (in the search box), `keybindingsSearchHasValue` (the search box has text), `keybindingFocus` (a row of the table has the focus), `whenFocus` (the box of the when-clause of a row has the focus) and `inputFocus` (any text box of the editor has the focus). The colors are `tree.tableColumnsBorder`, `tree.tableOddRowsBackground`, `keybindingTable.headerBackground` and `keybindingTable.rowsBackground`. No setting is added.
- The theme pickers (step 8.4, §8.4, §10.8) register `workbench.action.selectTheme` ("Color Theme", category Preferences, Ctrl+K Ctrl+T, weight of the workbench contributions) and `workbench.action.selectIconTheme` ("File Icon Theme", category Preferences, no key); both are in the palette ("Preferences: Color Theme", "Preferences: File Icon Theme"). The menu `ThemesSubMenu` has the rows "Color Theme" (order 1) and "File Icon Theme" (order 2), and is a submenu row "&&Themes" in the Preferences submenu of the File menu and "Themes" in the Manage menu, both in the group `2_configuration`, order 7 (after Settings and Keyboard Shortcuts). VS Code's third row, "Product Icon Theme", and its other theme commands are not registered. No context key and no setting is added: `workbench.colorTheme` (default "Dark Modern") and `workbench.iconTheme` (`string` or `null`, default `vs-seti`) were registered before; `window.autoDetectColorScheme`, `workbench.preferredDarkColorTheme` and `workbench.preferredLightColorTheme` act as in §8.4, and their UI (the button of the picker that opens them) is not built.
- The profile commands (step 8.6b, §10.12) register `workbench.profiles.actions.createProfile` ("Create Profile..."), `workbench.profiles.actions.switchProfile` ("Switch Profile..."), `workbench.profiles.actions.renameProfile` ("Rename Profile..."), `workbench.profiles.actions.deleteProfile` ("Delete Profile..."), `workbench.profiles.actions.exportProfile` ("Export Profile...") and `workbench.profiles.actions.importProfile` ("Import Profile..."), all in the category Profiles ("Profiles: Switch Profile...") and in the palette, with no key. The menu `ProfilesSubMenu` has their rows and is a submenu row "&&Profiles" in the Preferences submenu of the File menu and "Profiles" in the Manage menu, group `2_configuration`, order 1. The status bar item `status.profile` runs `switchProfile`. No context key and no setting is added.
- The window and the Explorer set `workbenchState` (`"folder"` or `"empty"`), `explorerViewletVisible`, `foldersViewVisible`, `explorerViewletFocus`, `filesExplorerFocus`, `openEditorsFocus`, `explorerResourceIsFolder`, `explorerResourceIsRoot`, `explorerResourceReadonly` and `groupFocusedInOpenEditors` (step 6.14, §10.8); the Close Folder row of the File menu and the views of the Explorer have their `when` on `workbenchState`.

### 11.3 Keybindings (`core/keybinding`)

- The default keymap is VS Code's Linux keymap for the commands Emetos has. VS Code registers its defaults in code (`registerKeybinding`/`KeybindingsRegistry` calls in `coreCommands.ts` and the contributions); each step that adds a command adds its default binding from there.
- `keybindings.json` entries: `key` (with chords such as `ctrl+k ctrl+c`), `command` (a leading `-` removes a default), `when`, `args`. A leading `^` in a default's command id means the key is not consumed. An entry whose key, command id or when-clause cannot be read is reported as a problem and skipped (VS Code keeps an entry with an unknown key as an unbound command, so a typo in a removal would remove every key of the command). The `[KeyCode]` spelling of keys is not supported.
- Keys are VS Code's `KeyCode`s; the resolver matches the string `ctrl+shift+alt+meta+<Key>` of a pressed chord (the UI name of the key, such as `K`, `LeftArrow`, `[`). A pressed sequence resolves to no match, more chords needed, or a command; of several bindings that match, the last one registered whose when-clause holds wins, after the sort by weight (core 0, contributions 100, workbench 200), command id and secondary-key order. The dispatcher (`keybinding.Dispatcher`) keeps the pending chords and forgets them after 5 seconds (`Expire`, called from a timer); a key that completes no binding ends chord mode and is consumed, and shows "The key combination (Ctrl+K, X) is not a command.". Keybindings made of a lone modifier ("shift shift") resolve, but the dispatcher does not yet detect the double press (it needs key-up events: the workbench step).
- A chord's first key shows "(Ctrl+K) was pressed. Waiting for second key of chord..." in the status bar (step 6.20: `Window.ShowStatusMessage`, the last item of the left side). The message goes when the chord is completed or aborted, and when the dispatcher forgets the chord after `ChordTimeout` (a timer of the window calls `LeaveChordMode`); the message of a key that is not a command stays 10 seconds, as in VS Code.
- A **recording mode** (`Dispatcher.SetRecorder`) hands every key press to a `Recorder` as a `Chord` and consumes it; nothing is resolved while a recorder is set, and the pending chords are forgotten. The keybindings editor uses it for the search box and for the box that defines a key.
- `Resolver.Replace` swaps the contents of a resolver in place, so that the menus, the status bar and the dispatcher, which hold the pointer, follow a change of `keybindings.json` at once. `Item.FileEntry` is the 1-based position of an item in `keybindings.json` (0 for a default); `UserKeybindingsPath` is `<config dir>/keybindings.json`.

**The keybindings editor as built (step 8.3; `core/keybinding/{model,search,conflicts,editing,defaultjson}.go`, `core/editorgroup/keybindingsinput.go`, `gui/keybindingsui`, `gui/kit/keycaps.go`, `gui/app/{keybindingspane,userkeys}.go`).** Ports of `keybindingsEditor.ts`, `keybindingsEditorModel.ts`, `keybindingsEditorContribution.ts`, `keybindingEditing.ts` and `defineKeybindingWidget.ts`. The commands, keys, context keys and colors are in §11.2.
- **The model** (`keybinding.Model`, `NewModel(defaults, user, commands)`). One row (`Row`) for each default or user keybinding of a command, after the removals (`-command` entries) are applied, and one row without a key for each command that has none (listed once). A row has the command id, its label (the title, with the category in front: "Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts"), the keybinding, the `when` text, the source (`Default` or `User`; a command that lost its default key shows its unbound row as `User`) and the position in the file (`FileEntry`). Commands whose id starts with `_` or `vscode.` and the `dev.` commands are left out. Rows are sorted as VS Code sorts them by name: keys first, then labelled commands, by label (`fuzzy.Collate`) and command id, user rows before default rows of the same command. Sorting by precedence is not built.
- **Search** (`Model.Fetch(text)`, a list of `Result`s with the ranges that matched in the label, id, when and source and the keys that matched). As VS Code's `KeybindingItemMatches`: the words of the text match the label (words, camel case or contiguous), the command id, the when-clause and the source; a text in quotes (`"ctrl+k"`) matches the keybinding exactly (the first chord, the whole sequence of a longer one); a word that is a key name (or modifier) matches the keys that have it. The filters are `@source:user`, `@source:default` (`system` is accepted as `default`), `@command:<id>` (with `+when:<clause>`) and `@keybinding:<keys>`; the filters of extensions are not built. The matches are drawn in the highlight color of lists, in the label, in the id, in the when text and on the key caps.
- **The page** (`keybindingsui.Editor`). A search box ("Type to search in keybindings") with two buttons, record keys (Alt+K: the box then shows the badge "Recording Keys" and the placeholder "Recording Keys. Press Escape to exit", and every press becomes the quoted text of the search, `"ctrl+shift+p"`, up to two chords; Escape ends it) and clear (Escape clears a search); a table with the columns Command, Keybinding, When and Source, a header, zebra rows, and the rows as a `kit.List` with its own heights (a row that matched by id shows the id on a second line). The keybinding is drawn as key caps (`kit.NewKeyCaps`, shared with the quick input). A hovered, selected or focused row shows the pencil (Change Keybinding) or, for a row without a key, the plus (Add Keybinding). A double click on a row (or Enter) defines its key; the secondary button opens the context menu: Copy, Copy Command ID, Copy Command Title, Change Keybinding..., Add Keybinding..., Remove Keybinding, Reset Keybinding (only for a row from the user's file), Change When Expression, Show Same Keybindings (the search becomes `"<keys>"`). The button "Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)" in the header opens `keybindings.json`. The view state (the search and the selected row) is kept with the input and comes back with the state of the window; the recording of keys is not kept.
- **Defining a key** (`define.go`). Enter or the pencil opens a box over the table: "Press desired key combination and then press ENTER.", the keys as text and as key caps, and the number of commands that already have the keys ("1 existing command has this keybinding", a click on it shows them in the table; at most four are listed). The dispatcher is in recording mode: every press is recorded (two chords at most, a lone modifier is an unfinished chord that the next press replaces; Backspace is a key, as in VS Code). Enter confirms, Escape clears the recorded keys and, with none, closes the box; a click outside closes it. Choosing the keys of the row it already has changes nothing. With conflicts (below) a dialog asks what to do.
- **Conflicts** (`Model.FindConflicts(keybinding, when, command)`). The rows of other commands with exactly the same sequence of chords, whose when-clauses can both hold: two clauses overlap unless one provably excludes the other (one implies the negation of the other, with `contextkey.Implies`); empty or equal clauses overlap, and clauses that cannot be compared overlap. VS Code lists every row with the same keys; keys that are a prefix of a longer sequence are not reported. The dialog "Keybinding conflicts" has the buttons Keep Both (the default), Overwrite and Cancel. Keep Both adds the entry. Overwrite adds it and removes the others: an entry of the user's file with those keys is deleted, a default one gets a `-command` entry. Cancel does nothing.
- **Editing `keybindings.json`** (`keybinding.Editing`, each operation takes the text and gives the new text; the editor applies it as a minimal text edit, so comments and layout stay). Entries are written with the keys `key`, `command`, `when`, `args` in this order, indented as the file is (else by `editor.tabSize` and `editor.insertSpaces`); a file with comments only gets the array appended, an empty file or a missing one becomes `// Place your key bindings in this file to override the defaults` and `[]`. A file with syntax errors is not edited (`KeybindingsEditFileInvalid`), nor one whose root is not an array (`KeybindingsEditNotArray`).
  - Add (`Add`): appends `{ "key", "command", "when", "args" }`; the `when` and `args` are those of the row (the arguments of a default are carried to the new entry).
  - Change (`Edit`, a row with a key): a row from the user's file is changed in place (its `key`, found by `FileEntry` and checked against the command); a default row gets a new entry and the removal `{ "key": "<old key>", "command": "-<command>", "when": "<old when>" }` (not repeated when it is there).
  - Change the when-clause (`UpdateWhen`): the same, for the `when`; the clause is checked first (`ValidateWhen`: "Not a when-clause: ..." is shown under the box and nothing is written). An empty text removes the `when`.
  - Remove (`Remove`): a row from the user's file loses its entry; a default one gets the removal entry.
  - Reset (`Reset`): every entry of the command in the user's file, its removals included, is deleted, so the defaults come back.
  - Errors: the tags of `core/jsonc` (a text edit failed), `KeybindingEditKeyMissing`, `KeybindingEditCommandMissing`, `KeybindingEditUnbound` (a row without a key cannot be changed or removed), `KeybindingEntryNotFound` (the entry of the row is not in the file any more), `KeybindingsFileWriteFailed`, `KeybindingsFileCreateFailed` and `KeybindingsInputInvalid`. A failed edit is logged and shown as an error notification.
- **The file in the window** (`userKeys`). `keybindings.json` is read when the window opens and again when it changes (the watcher, a document of it that is saved, an edit of the editor); the resolver of the window is replaced in place (`Resolver.Replace`) and any chord in progress is dropped, so the keys, the menus and the status bar follow at once. An entry that cannot be read is skipped and logged (§11.3 above). As the settings (§11.1 "Settings in an open editor"): when a document of the file is open, the edit goes into it and it is saved when it was not dirty; a dirty document stays dirty and the disk is left alone (VS Code refuses to edit a dirty `keybindings.json`; Emetos edits the document); with no document the file is written (keeping its encoding, line ends and BOM) and made when it does not exist. The keys of a dirty document count when it is saved.
- **The JSON commands.** `openGlobalKeybindingsFile` makes `keybindings.json` when it is not there and opens it as a text editor. `openDefaultKeybindingsFile` opens the read-only document `emetos-virtual:/defaultKeybindings.json` (language `jsonc`, tab "Default Keybindings") with `keybinding.DefaultKeybindingsJSON`: the header comment and an array with every default keybinding in VS Code's layout (`{ "key": "ctrl+,",   "command": "workbench.action.openSettings" }`, the `when` and `args` on the next lines), without VS Code's comment with the title of each entry.
- **Not built**: the sort by precedence, the actions "Show Default/User/System Keybindings", the history of the search, resizable columns, auto-completion in the when box, editing of `args`, the JSON editor widget that VS Code's `editor.action.defineKeybinding` shows in a text editor, the commands that accept or reject the when box (Enter and Escape in the box do that), the actions in the title of the editor and the filters of extensions.

## 12. Privacy

- Emetos sends nothing about the user anywhere on its own: no telemetry, crash reports or update checks. Network access is allowed for what the user asks of a feature or an extension (an extension that talks to a service, a remote workspace, a link opened in the browser); the archtest no longer forbids network packages (the rules `NetworkImport` and `NetOutsideIPC` were removed on 2026-10-25 at the user's request).
- Links in notifications or help open in the user's browser through the desktop portal, only on a click.
- The camera is read only while the Scan QR Code dialog is open (§10.18, step 15.5), and no frame of it is kept, written or sent; Show My Public Key as QR Code draws a public key only.
- Logs stay on disk (§13).

## 13. Errors and logging

- Every error uses `github.com/rm4n0s/errors` (CLAUDE.md). Errors shown to the user become notifications with a short message; the full error goes to the log as a `slog` attribute (`"err", err`).
- **Routes** (step 9.9). An error is built once, in the function that detects the failure, with a literal Tag, and travels up unchanged; no function exists only to build an error for its callers, and no sentinel is made with `errors.New` at package level (§5.3, `internal/archtest`). Every Tag is asserted by a test from the entry function down to the Tag (`HasRoute("Entry.Func->Inner.Func.Tag")`, or `appErr.Tag`), and a Tag that truly cannot be tested is listed with its reason in `docs/ERROR-TAGS-UNTESTED.md` (the one exception list, a line `- \`Tag\`: reason` each). A failure that a healthy system never produces is reached through a small seam of the package under test (an option or an injectable function, never a global).
- Logs: `log/slog` to `$XDG_STATE_HOME/emetos/logs/<date>/main.log` (kept 7 days), and to the "Emetos" channel of the Output panel (§10.13: `logs.Store` has `Subscribe`, `Watch` and `Clear`). `emetos --log debug` raises the level.
- A panic in a background goroutine is recovered, logged, and reported once as an error notification; the window stays open. A panic in the UI goroutine is handled by Glutter's error reporting, logged, and Emetos tries to write backups (§10.10) before exiting.

## 14. Performance targets

Measured on release builds (`-tags glutter_release,emetos_dev`, so dev commands can drive the app) on the user's machine, in their desktop session with its GPU; headless numbers (software rendering) are recorded too but don't decide. The numbers and the method go in `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`.

| Metric | Target | First measured |
|---|---|---|
| Typing a character in a 10,000-line Go file: UI-thread time of the frame that shows it | < 4 ms | step 3.11 (no highlighting), again with highlighting in step 4.9 |
| Scrolling a 100,000-line file: frames | display refresh rate, no UI-thread frame over 8 ms | 3.11 |
| Opening a 10 MB file: first frame with text | < 300 ms with the GPU; headless, < 300 ms over the first frame of an empty window (step 10.1: 110 to 140 ms) | 3.11 |
| Opening a 200 MB file in large file mode: first frame with text | < 3 s | 5.12 |
| Cold start with no folder, to the first frame | < 400 ms with the GPU; Emetos's own share (before the window plus the first build) < 100 ms, also with restored tabs (step 10.1: 21 to 28 ms, 76 to 77 ms with four tabs). Headless starts spend 560 to 620 ms in Glutter trying Vulkan first, which its owner decided to keep (Glutter's SPEC §9.6): the headless runs of `scripts/proof.sh` and `scripts/perf.sh` set `GLUTTER_RENDERER=gles` (not with `--session`), and the figure of the session is the one that decides | 3.11, again with the workbench in 10.1 |
| Idle, window focused, cursor blinking | < 1% of a core with the GPU; headless, where llvmpipe's threads dominate, at most 2 frames a second (`TestIdleWorkbenchDrawsOnlyTheBlink`); no frames at all when the window has no focus | 3.11, 10.1 |
| Resident memory, one 10,000-line file open | no more than an empty Glutter window (its `counter` example) plus 150 MB (revised in step 10.1 from plus 50 MB: Emetos's Go runtime alone is about 50 MB more than the counter's; measured 418 MB against 280 MB headless after the fix of the tab font); earlier: measured 271 MB against the baseline's 287 MB headless, where Mesa's software GL dominates (revised in step 3.11 from "< 200 MB", which the graphics stack alone exceeds; the number to hold is the one with the GPU, `scripts/perf.sh --session`) | 3.11 |
| Fuzzy file search over 100,000 paths, per keystroke | < 30 ms, off the UI thread | 6.16 (the scorer alone: 9 to 19 ms), 6.18 (the search end to end: 2 to 8 ms on all cores, 9 to 27 ms on one; the listing of the folder: 800,000 files a second) |
| Markdown preview of a 700 KB document with 150 images (the size of `docs/IMPLEMENTED.md` in October 2026) | opening: the first frame of the preview within 300 ms; resident memory at most 200 MB more than with the file open as text; scrolling: no frame (UI thread and raster) over 16 ms with the GPU. Measured before 17b.2 on the user's desktop: 1.6 GB more, 1.2 to 1.65 s per frame; headless: 9.2 s to the first frame, 2.1 GB more, 0.8 s of raster per frame. After 17b.2, headless (`docs/PERFORMANCE.md`): the first blocks 160 to 260 ms after the command, 116 to 129 MB more, the UI thread 0.8 ms per frame on average (the frame of a jump 40 ms); the GPU numbers wait for the pass on the desktop | 17b.2 |
| Idle allocation, window focused, cursor blinking, a 10,000-line file open | Emetos's part of a blink frame (the UI thread without the renderer: build, layout, paint and the scene) at most 6 KB and 120 allocations, pinned by `TestIdleBlinkFrameAllocationStaysInBudget` (measured: 4.6 KB and 92 allocations, 8.0 KB and 147 before the fixes of step 17b.4). The renderer's part is Glutter's and not a target of Emetos's: headless, 1.9 MB and 7,900 allocations a frame (about 4 MB a second) with the Go file, 8.4 MB and 30,000 a frame (17 MB a second) with the Markdown preview open (`docs/PERFORMANCE.md` "Idle allocation"; `docs/GLUTTER-ISSUES.md` "The renderers flatten the whole scene every frame"). It is garbage that a collection frees every 5 to 10 s (the live heap is flat), not growth; the desktop figure (2.5 to 5 MB a frame, about 11 MB a second) is the same renderer with more text on screen | 17b.4 |
| Terminal output: 10 MB of text written to a terminal (`cat` of a file) | processed in under 2 s with no frame (UI thread and raster) over 33 ms; a key typed at a shell prompt drawn within one frame | 17d.2 |

**As built (step 17b.4).**

- *The idle frame.* A profile of the idle window (release build with `emetos_dev`, `scripts/headless-wayland.sh`, `scripts/isolated.sh`, `EMETOS_PROFILE_DIR`, `SIGUSR1`; `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` "Idle allocation") put 99% of what a blink frame allocates in Glutter's renderer (`gpu.Flatten` expands every glyph of the scene on every frame, also inside the layers its raster cache holds) and under 1% in Emetos and the framework. The blink repaints only the layer of the cursors (a repaint boundary of its own) and adds one picture to the scene, as a test that walks the scenes shows. What Emetos could fix, it fixed: that layer read the text of every visible row on every blink to look for control characters (57 allocations, 3.4 KB a frame); `controlCache` (`internal/gui/editor/display_paint.go`) keeps the marks of the rows and reads a row again only when the document (its version), `editor.stopRenderingLineAfter` or what the row shows changed, and a frame that changes nothing allocates nothing. The renderer's cost is written down in `docs/GLUTTER-ISSUES.md` with the fix Glutter should make. Decision: the budget is on Emetos's part, which a test with the fake platform can see (it has no renderer): 6 KB and 120 allocations a blink frame in the whole workbench with a 10,000-line highlighted Go file, which is 1.3 times the measurement and fails the state before the fixes; the renderer's numbers are recorded, not bounded, because Emetos cannot change them.
- *The gesture arena.* Glutter 1.9.1 can end the process with `index out of range [0] with length 0` (`gestures/arena.go:309`) when pointer events that waited for a slow frame are dispatched in one go: the Linux platform gives every mouse event the pointer id 0, and the arena's default resolution is posted to the next turn of the event loop. Emetos cannot avoid the trigger (every tap target is a lone member of an arena that the mouse can move away from), so `fixGestureArena` (`internal/gui/app/arenafix.go`) gives each binding (the window's, under the tray host, and each headless view's) an arena manager whose microtasks run before the next pointer event is dispatched (`OnDispatchEvent`); the reproduction, passing with it and panicking without it, is in `arenafix_test.go`. The entries of this and of the two other Glutter bugs of the milestone (the renderer's draws outside the clip and fingerprint of every path, the keyboard's error log of "no keymap") are in `docs/GLUTTER-ISSUES.md`; the keyboard one has no workaround.

## 15. Testing

### 15.1 Tests

- Core packages: table-driven unit tests, fuzz tests for the buffer (random edits checked against a plain string), the JSONC parser, the snippet parser, the when-clause parser, and the tokenizer (no panics, bounded time).
- **Ported VS Code tests** use 1-based lines and UTF-16 columns; `core/vstest` converts them to Emetos positions. A case with non-ASCII text has its expected positions worked out again for byte columns, with a comment saying so. A case that needs VS Code's TypeScript harness (a full editor, services) is skipped, and the count of skipped cases is recorded.
- Tokenization: VS Code's own oracle, `extensions/vscode-colorize-tests/test/colorize-fixtures` and `colorize-results` (scopes per token), for every bundled language that has fixtures there; small fixtures of Emetos's own for the others.
- UI: `gluttertest` widget tests with the fake platform (keys through `SendKeyEvent`, IME through `SendTextInputEvent`, clipboard, file choosers, window close), and golden images with `MatchesGolden`.
- Golden images need deterministic fonts: UI tests load Go Mono (regular, bold, italic, bold italic), Codicons and Seti through `gluttertest.Opts.Fonts`, and set `editor.fontFamily` to Go Mono (D14). Glyphs Go Mono lacks (CJK, emoji) show as boxes, so their layout is checked through the paragraph queries, not by goldens.
- **Isolation**: no test, proof or check reads or writes the user's real configuration, state, cache, trash or socket. Go tests call a helper that points every `XDG_*` variable at `t.TempDir()` (`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, where the socket and its lock live, at a short folder of its own, since a socket path is limited to 107 bytes); the two-process tests of `core/ipc` start copies of the test binary (`EMETOS_IPC_HELPER` makes `TestMain` run only the ipc code, with no window) in their own process groups under a deadline, and kill the groups when the test ends; scripts run the app through `scripts/isolated.sh`, which does the same with a temporary folder (and can copy a fixture configuration in). `scripts/proof.sh --launch '<args>'` (repeatable; step 9b.3) runs `emetos <args>` once more for each launch inside the same isolated environment and compositor, after the first instance listens on its socket (`scripts/run-with-launches.sh`), so that the run is handed over to the first instance over the real socket of the private runtime folder; the default `--after` is then 1 s, so that the capture comes after the hand-over.
- Display tests (`emetos_display` tag) start the real app under a headless Wayland compositor.
- **Real input** (step 17b.1, after the desktop test of 2026-10-27 found bugs that every widget test missed): `internal/testenv/realinput` types and clicks through the compositor, with a Wayland virtual keyboard (`zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1`, one keyboard for the whole run) and a virtual pointer, so keys reach Emetos as a real keyboard's do (`wl_keyboard`, then Glutter's key and text input path), which the fake platform's `SendKeyEvent` skips. Display tests use it under the headless compositor; every input box has such a test, and a fix of a UI bug comes with one that was seen failing first. `scripts/realinput.sh --desktop` runs the same in a nested sway window on the user's desktop: a milestone that changes the UI is published only after the manager's pass there (its screenshots viewed, the GPU numbers of §14 measured). The window has to stay visible: a hidden one gets no frames.
- **Real input as built (step 17b.1).** `internal/testenv/realinput` (standard library and `rm4n0s/errors`) is the Wayland client: `Connect` makes **one** virtual keyboard (`zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1`, a US xkb keymap in a sealed memfd, kept for the life of the client) and one virtual pointer (`zwlr_virtual_pointer_v1`); `Type`, `Press("ctrl+shift+v", "Escape", "f2")`, `Click`, `DoubleClick`, `RightClick`, `Drag`, `Scroll`, each followed by a `wl_display.sync` round trip and a key delay of 10 ms; pointer positions are window coordinates (`SetWindow` from sway's IPC: `SwayWindowOf` gives the window's content rectangle by pid, `SwayLayout` the bounding box of the outputs, which the absolute motion is counted against; the IPC is spoken directly over `$SWAYSOCK`). `internal/testenv/display` (tag `emetos_display`) is the harness of the tests: `Start(t, Options)` builds `./cmd/emetos` once per test process (cgo-free, a debug build so dev commands exist; `EMETOS_DISPLAY_BINARY` names a prebuilt one), starts it in its own process group with an environment made from scratch (temporary `HOME` and `XDG_*`, a short private `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` with a link to the compositor's socket, `GLUTTER_RENDERER=gles`, no session bus), after connecting the virtual keyboard, waits for the window and the dev server, focuses the window, and stops everything in `t.Cleanup` (SIGTERM to the group, then SIGKILL; the virtual devices last). `App` has `Type`, `Press`, `Click`, `ClickInput`, `DoubleClick`, `RightClick`, `Scroll`, `Drag`, `Dev`, `Inputs`, `Focused`, `Editor`, `Settle`, `Eventually`, `WaitFocusedText`, `Screenshot` (grim, cropped to the window). The editor handles the events a moment after the compositor sent them, so a test waits with `Eventually`/`WaitFocusedText` for what a key did and `Settle`s before a negative check. The tests of the inputs are in `cmd/emetos/realinput_display_test.go` (`scripts/headless-wayland.sh -- go test -race -tags emetos_display ./cmd/emetos`). `scripts/realinput.sh [--desktop] [--shots dir] [-- go test args]` runs them in a headless sway, or with `--desktop` in a nested sway window on the user's desktop; the tests then get the nested sway's socket and IPC only (a private runtime folder), never the desktop's. Step 17b.3 adds `cmd/emetos/editing_display_test.go`: typing in the editor (brackets, completions, signature help) against the fake language server (`lsptest`) started as `go.goplsPath` through a one-line launcher; `TestRealInputTypingOver...`, `TestRealInputCompletionWith...` and `TestRealInputSignatureHelp...` read `dev.editor` (`inSnippet`, `tabStops`, `suggestVisible`, `signatureVisible`).
- Performance benchmarks (§14) are Go benchmarks plus `scripts/perf.sh`, which runs the app with `GLUTTER_FRAME_STATS=1`.

### 15.2 Dev commands

`EMETOS_DEV_COMMANDS` holds a JSON array of steps run after the first frame, each `["<command id>", <args>]` or `["sleep", "<duration>"]`, for example `[["workbench.action.quickOpen", ">line"], ["sleep", "200ms"]]`. Any registered command can be used; commands whose id starts with `dev.` exist only for this (opening a file at a position in a group, posting a notification, typing text) and are registered only in debug and `emetos_dev` builds (D15). `dev.openFile {"path", "line", "column", "group", "preview"}` shows a file in an editor group of the window (a relative path is relative to the folder Emetos runs in; line and column count from 1 and are optional; `group` is the place of an existing group, counted from 1 in the order the groups appear in the grid, and the file opens in the active group when it is not given; the group becomes the active group; a `group` that is not a whole number of 1 or more fails with the tag `DevOpenFileInvalid`, and one that does not exist with `DevOpenFileGroupInvalid`; `"preview": true` opens it as the preview editor of the group (an italic tab that the next preview replaces; only with `workbench.editor.enablePreview` and for a document without changes), as a navigation does, where the default is a kept editor, and a `preview` that is not true or false fails with `DevOpenFilePreviewInvalid`); `dev.openDiff {"original", "modified"}` opens a diff editor over two documents in the active group (step 9.5; each side is an absolute path, a path relative to the folder of the window, a `file://` URI, an `emetos-virtual:` URI whose provider generates the text, or the `untitled:` URI of an open untitled document; no folder and a relative path fails with `DevOpenDiffInvalid`, as do missing or empty arguments, an untitled document that is not open fails with `DevOpenDiffSideMissing`, and a side that cannot be opened fails with that side's tag, leaving the other side unused); `dev.openMergeEditor {"path"}` opens a file with conflict markers in the merge editor of the active group (step 9.8; the argument may also be the path as a string; a relative path is relative to the folder of the window, or to the folder Emetos runs in when none is open; the file is read and the merge made at once, so the next step of a script finds the merge editor; a file whose merge editor is open is activated; the form `{"input1", "input2", "base", "result"}` opens the four files as `emetos --merge` does, read in the background; arguments that are neither fail with the tag `DevOpenMergeInvalid`, a working folder that is gone with `DevOpenMergePathFailed`, a file without a complete conflict with `MergeMarkersNotFound`); `dev.acceptMerge {"conflict", "side"}` resolves a conflict of the merge editor of the active group as the actions above it do (step 9.8; `conflict` counts the conflicts from 0, `side` is `"incoming"`, `"current"`, `"both"` (current, then incoming) or `"base"`; arguments that are not an object fail with `DevAcceptMergeInvalid`, a conflict that is not a whole number from 0 with `DevAcceptMergeConflictInvalid`, another side with `DevAcceptMergeSideInvalid`, no merge editor with `DevAcceptMergeNoEditor`, a conflict that is not there with `MergeConflictIndexInvalid`); `dev.switchProfile {"name"}` gives the workspace of the active tab another profile in place (step 8.6, `Workspace.SwitchProfile`; the argument may also be the name as a string; "Default" or any capitalization of the name of a profile that exists, which it does not make; no name fails with the tag `DevSwitchProfileInvalid`, a profile that does not exist with `ProfileSwitchNotFound`); `dev.openFolderInNewTab {"path"}` opens a folder in a new workspace tab after the active one, which becomes the active tab (step 9b.1; it replaces `dev.openFolderInNewWindow` of step 7.8; the argument may also be the path as a string; a relative path is relative to the working directory of the process; a folder that is open makes its tab the active one; the tab is made whatever `window.openFoldersInNewWindow` says; an argument that is not a path fails with the tag `DevOpenFolderInvalid`, a folder that is not there with the tags of `workspace.Open`); `dev.openWindowTab {"kind"}` opens a window tab of an extension after the active tab and makes it the active one (step 11.7; the argument may also be the id of the kind, such as `emetos.scratchpad.tab`; no kind fails with the tag `DevOpenWindowTabInvalid`, a kind no extension has with `WindowTabKindUnknown`, a kind whose extension is turned off with `WindowTabKindDisabled`); `dev.openPlusMenu` opens the menu of the "+" button of the strip, as a click on it does (step 11.7; with no strip on screen it fails with `DevOpenPlusMenuUnavailable`); `dev.activateWindowTab {"index"}` makes the tab at a place of the strip, counted from 0, the active tab (step 9b.1; the argument may also be the number; an argument that is not a whole number from 0 fails with `DevActivateWindowTabInvalid`, a place with no tab with `DevActivateWindowTabMissing`); each later step of the script runs in the workspace of the tab that is active then, so `[["dev.openFolderInNewTab",{"path":"..."}],["dev.openFile",{"path":"..."}]]` opens the file in the new tab; `dev.openMenu {"id", "x", "y"}` opens a menu of the window (step 6.7): the id of a menu of the menu bar (`MenubarEditMenu`: opened as a click on its title does), `GlobalActivity` (the Manage menu) or `EditorContext` (the context menu of the editor, at `x` and `y` in window coordinates, 400 and 250 by default; the argument may also be the id as a string); an id of any other menu, and a menu of the bar that has no item, fail; `dev.notify {"severity", "message", "source", "actions", "progress"}` sends a notification through `core/notify` (step 6.11; the argument may also be the message as a string): `severity` is `"info"` (the default), `"warning"` or `"error"`, `message` is a text that is not empty, `source` a text, `actions` a list of button labels (a button closes the toast and writes `dev.notify action` with the label to the log) and `progress` a number from 0 to 100 (the bar of a running progress) or `"infinite"`; a bad argument fails with its own tag, `DevNotifyArgumentsInvalid`, `DevNotifySeverityInvalid`, `DevNotifyMessageInvalid`, `DevNotifySourceInvalid`, `DevNotifyActionsInvalid` or `DevNotifyProgressInvalid`; `dev.setMarkers {"owner", "resource", "markers": [{"severity", "message", "startLine", "startColumn", "endLine", "endColumn", "source", "code"}]}` sets the markers an owner (`"dev"` by default) has for a file, so that the Problems panel has something to show before area 3 (step 6.12; the window implements it; `resource` is a path, relative to the folder Emetos runs in or absolute; a missing or empty `markers` removes the markers of the owner for that file; `severity` is `"error"` (the default), `"warning"`, `"info"` or `"hint"`, `message` a text that is not empty, the four positions whole numbers from 1 (1, 1, the start line and the start column when missing), `source` and `code` texts); a bad argument fails with its own tag, `DevSetMarkersArgumentsInvalid`, `DevSetMarkersOwnerInvalid`, `DevSetMarkersResourceInvalid`, `DevSetMarkersCwdFailed`, `DevSetMarkersMarkersInvalid`, `DevSetMarkersMarkerInvalid`, `DevSetMarkersSeverityInvalid`, `DevSetMarkersMessageInvalid`, `DevSetMarkersPositionInvalid` or `DevSetMarkersTextInvalid`, and without a window it fails with `DevNoWindow`; `dev.showHover {"line", "column"}` shows the hover of the editor that has the focus at a position counted from 1 (the cursor when missing) and keeps it until the cursor moves (step 12.4; nothing there fails with the tag `DevShowHoverEmpty`); `dev.agents.replay {"fixture"}` plays a recorded stream of the agent's program into a session tab with no program (step 13.2; the extension registers it, §10.16 "As built (step 13.2)"; the path is relative to the folder Emetos runs in; a missing argument fails with the tag `ReplayFixtureInvalid`, a file that cannot be read with `ReplayFixtureUnreadable`, a line that is not a message with `ReplayFixtureInvalid` or the adapter's `MessageInvalid`); `dev.log {"channel", "message"}` appends a line to a log channel of the Output panel (`"Emetos"` by default; the argument may also be the message as a string), and fails with `DevLogArgumentsInvalid`, `DevLogChannelInvalid` or `DevLogMessageInvalid`; `dev.type` (a text, one character in each frame) and `dev.scroll` act on the editor that has the focus. The runner waits two frames after each command, so that what the command made (an editor, the focus) is there for the next. The keyboard focus of a new active group follows a few frames later (§10.3), so a script that types after a command that changes the group puts a `sleep` between them.

**The dev server and the read-only dev commands** (step 17b.1, `gui/app/devserver.go`, `devquery.go`). In a build that runs dev commands, `EMETOS_DEV_SOCKET` names a Unix socket (mode 0600; a stale file is replaced) that the process listens on for its whole life. A client writes a JSON line `{"command": "<id>", "args": <argument>}` and reads a line `{"ok": true, "result": ...}` or `{"ok": false, "tag": "<error tag>", "error": "<message>"}`; the command runs on the UI thread in the workspace of the active tab, and the answer comes two frames later, as for the steps of `EMETOS_DEV_COMMANDS`. A request that is not valid JSON, or has no command, answers with the tag `DevRequestInvalid`. The read-only commands give their answer through the context of the request, so they do nothing in a script: `dev.inputs` lists the text fields on screen (`text`, `selectionStart`, `selectionEnd`, `focused`, `readOnly` and their place in window coordinates), failing with `DevInputsNoWindow` before the window is up; `dev.editor` gives the document of the active editor (`path`, `uri`, `text`, `dirty`, the primary cursor as `line` and `column` from 1, and from step 17b.3 `inSnippet`, `tabStops` (the tab stops of the snippet session that the document holds), `suggestVisible` and `signatureVisible`), failing with `DevEditorNoWorkspace` and `DevEditorNone`. `dev.markdown` (step 17b.2) lists the Markdown previews on screen (`blocks`, `built`, `builds`, `measured`, `parsing`, `topLine`, `scrollTop`, `contentHeight`, `imageBytes` and `images` of their image cache, and their place `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`), failing with `DevMarkdownNoWindow`.

**Profiling** (step 10.1, `cmd/emetos/profile_dev.go`, only in builds with the `emetos_dev` tag): with `EMETOS_PROFILE_DIR` set to a folder, `SIGUSR1` writes `heap-N.pprof` (after a garbage collection), `allocs-N.pprof`, `goroutines-N.txt` and `memstats-N.txt` there, `SIGUSR2` starts a CPU profile and the next `SIGUSR2` ends it (`cpu-N.pprof`), and `EMETOS_PROFILE_START=cpu` (with `EMETOS_PROFILE_HZ`, 1000 by default) starts one at once, for the start of the process. `GODEBUG=memprofilerate=1` samples every allocation, the start included. `scripts/perf.sh --profile <dir>` does it for its measuring times (`docs/PERFORMANCE.md`).

## 16. Build and runtime requirements

- Build: Go 1.27 only. `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./cmd/emetos` makes the binary; users build with `-tags glutter_release` (D16).
- Run: what Glutter needs (Wayland or X11, Vulkan or OpenGL ES, fontconfig), a monospace font, and optionally xdg-desktop-portal for file dialogs and opening links. The system tray needs a StatusNotifier host (GNOME: the AppIndicator extension, §10.14).
- Version: `emetos --version` prints the module version of the build (`go install ...@v0.1.0` gives `v0.1.0`; a build in a checkout gets Go's stamp, the tag on a clean tagged commit or a pseudo-version such as `v0.0.0-<date>-<revision>+dirty` otherwise; a build with no stamp (`go run`, `-buildvcs=false`) gives `v0.1.0-dev`, the constant `devVersion` of `cmd/emetos`, which changes only when the next development cycle starts). Releases are tagged `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` by the maintainer; the first is `v0.1.0` (areas 1 and 2, step 10.2).
- **Desktop entry and icon** (step 10.2). `assets/dev.emetos.Emetos.desktop` (`Exec=emetos %F`, `Icon` and `StartupWMClass` are the application id `dev.emetos.Emetos` that `gui/app` gives Glutter as `AppID`, categories `Development;TextEditor;IDE;`, text types and `inode/directory`) and `scripts/install-desktop.sh [--exec <program>] [--uninstall]`, which copies the entry to `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/applications/` (with the absolute path of the program in `Exec`, because a launcher often lacks `go install`'s folder in its `PATH`) and `assets/icons/emetos-<N>.png` to `.../icons/hicolor/<N>x<N>/apps/dev.emetos.Emetos.png`; it runs `update-desktop-database` and `gtk-update-icon-cache` when they are installed and writes nowhere else. The icons are not committed twice: the script makes the theme layout. Tests: `assets/icons/desktop_test.go` (the entry's keys, `desktop-file-validate` when installed, the script against a private data folder with fake and without cache tools, and the uninstall) and `internal/gui/app/appicon_test.go` (`AppID` is the name of the entry).

## 17. Licensing and third-party assets

Emetos is MIT-licensed (`LICENSE`). The reference sources are pinned in `scripts/reference-versions.txt` (committed). Bundled assets are listed in `NOTICE`, each with its license in `third_party/<name>/`:

| Asset | Source | License |
|---|---|---|
| TextMate grammars and language configurations | VS Code `extensions/*`; each grammar's upstream is listed in VS Code's `cgmanifest.json` files | MIT, and the grammar's own license (checked per grammar when it is added; a grammar without a permissive license is left out and recorded) |
| Color themes | VS Code `extensions/theme-defaults` | MIT |
| Ported code, default keybindings and setting defaults | VS Code `src/vs` | MIT |
| TextMate tokenizer algorithms | `microsoft/vscode-textmate` | MIT |
| Go module grammar | `golang/vscode-go` | MIT |
| Emmet parser algorithms and snippets | `emmetio/emmet` | MIT |
| Seti file icons (font and mapping) | VS Code `extensions/theme-seti` | MIT |
| Codicons (font and `codicon.csv`) | npm package `@vscode/codicons` | CC BY 4.0 (icons), MIT (code) |
| Application icon (`assets/icons/emetos-<size>.png`) | Drawn for Emetos with Glutter's canvas (`kit.AppIconPainter`, step 9b.4); the PNG files are what the test of `internal/gui/kit` renders from it | The project's own work, under its license (MIT, `LICENSE`); no third-party artwork or font is in it |
| vscode-textmate license | `microsoft/vscode-textmate` `LICENSE.md`, copied to `third_party/vscode-textmate/` (the algorithms are ported, no file is bundled) | MIT |
| Go modules linked into the binary | Glutter (BSD-3-Clause), `rm4n0s/errors`, `regexp2` (MIT), `go-text/typesetting` (Unlicense or BSD-3-Clause), `golang.org/x/*` (BSD-3-Clause), `purego` (Apache-2.0), `godbus/dbus` (BSD-2-Clause) | Listed in `NOTICE`; the license files come with the module sources |
| Go Mono (tests only, not bundled) | `golang.org/x/image/font/gofont` | BSD-3-Clause |
| `scripts/headless-wayland.sh`, `scripts/screenshot-headless.sh` | Glutter | BSD-3-Clause |

## 20. Risks

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Text rendering through Glutter is too slow for an editor | Per-line paragraph cache, repaint boundary for the text, the performance check in step 3.11 before anything else is built on the editor; fixes go into Glutter (D8). Glutter's own numbers (41–58 µs per cold code line, 5–10 µs for an unchanged one) fit the budget of §14 |
| TextMate grammars written for Oniguruma behave differently with regexp2 | Translation layer in `core/regex`, a test that compiles every pattern of every bundled grammar, VS Code's colorize oracles, timeouts |
| Glutter is young; Emetos is its first large app | Workarounds are marked and listed (D8); Glutter fixes are made in the Glutter repository; step 9b.1b took the fixes of Glutter 1.7 into use and removed their workarounds, and the fixes of Glutter 1.8 and 1.8.1 (the fonts, the tree's nodes, the title bar's gestures, the error boundary of the extension's box) were taken the same way |
| The close button of the window cannot be told from the application's own request to exit | Glutter 1.7 gives `WindowingOwner.SetImplicitWindowDelegate`: the delegate is asked when the user closes the first window, and without one the close is a request to exit. With one window (step 9b.1) that request is a quit over every tab, which is what the close button does without a tray; step 9b.4 set the delegate to hide the window on the close button, and `Workspaces.closeButton` quits as before when no tray is shown or `window.closeToTray` is off |
| GNOME shows no tray icons without the AppIndicator extension | The close button quits when no tray is shown (`TrayUnavailable`, which Glutter reports once, soon after the start, through the error reporter: `Workspaces.errorReporter` notes it, logs it at info level and shows the window if it was hidden meanwhile), so a window is never lost; the README says how to get the extension. Confirmed by the tests with a session bus that is not there (the close button quits, one log entry, no notification); the real GNOME case is the manual check of step 9b.4 |
| The scope of "what VS Code has" grows | Areas 3–11 are outside this spec until planned; every feature in §3 is a row with a defined behavior |
